title: China’s rise has made Indian Ocean Region a contested arena of geopolitical uncertainties: Navy Chief
content: Warning that economic prosperity and maritime security are now inseparable, Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan said on Saturday that the Indian Ocean is no longer just a vital trade route and China's rapid military and economic expansion reshaped the strategic Indian Ocean Region (IOR), turning it into a contested space and arena of geopolitical uncertainty and great-power rivalry. Speaking on 'Oceans of Influence' at the Manorama News Conclave at Lulu Bolgatty International Convention Centre in Kochi, Admiral Swaminathan detailed how global power dynamics have pivoted toward Asia and the Indo-Pacific, placing the IOR directly at the heart of international strategic calculations. China has grown astoundingly fast – faster than all of us thought, certainly much faster than all of us liked. China is a threat to many countries; China is a challenge for us. And so, the Indian Ocean Region continues to be contested; it continues to be very, very competitive, he said. He said that the region has been at the centre of global security concerns since 2008, after the 9/11 attacks. The intensifying rivalry among major powers has now added another layer of unpredictability, requiring the Indian Navy to constantly expand its operational footprint, capabilities and technological sophistication. Against the backdrop of China's rise, the Admiral stressed that India, as an independent nation with an independent navy, monitors the security environment on a daily basis and prepares politically and operationally for any eventuality. The Indian Navy is a growing force, and it is ready to face any evolving challenges. We plan to grow in terms of our capability, numbers, and sophistication of the systems we have, so that while our threats and challenges continue to become more serious, our capabilities also grow commensurately, so that we can protect our national interests at all times, he said. Swaminathan added that the navy's response is built around maintaining an uninterrupted watch over the Indian Ocean. The Indian Navy has kept two warships – one in the Gulf of Aden and another in the Gulf of Oman – continuously deployed on station since the 26/11 attacks. At the Information Fusion Centre – Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR) in Gurugram, thousands of ships are tracked every day through pattern analysis, including their itineraries, cargo profiles and ports of call. This is complemented by round-the-clock aerial and naval surveillance of key maritime chokepoints, including the Strait of Hormuz. The importance of that vigilance became particularly clear during the recent West Asia crisis. Swaminathan pointed out that disruptions at sea can quickly translate into economic consequences on land. Nearly 40% of India's crude oil, more than 50% of its urea, and close to half of its LPG and LNG imports were vulnerable to disruptions. The navy deployed a task force near the Strait of Hormuz and safely escorted more than 34 merchant vessels carrying critical cargo worth over 15,000 crore since the issue started in the Strait of Hormuz. India is the only country that has brought out the largest number of ships from the Strait of Hormuz, he said. Ocean beneath India's economic rise For India, maritime security is also inseparable from economic ambition. Swaminathan said the oceans would be a fundamental enabler of India's journey from a $4-trillion economy to a developed nation by 2047. Quoting 16th-century Ottoman Admiral Barbarossa, as cited by Indian strategic thinker Sardar K M Panikkar in his 1945 work 'India and the Indian Ocean', he reiterated: He who rules on the sea will shortly rule on land. Nearly 95% of India's trade by volume and almost 70% by value moves by sea, he said. The seabed is equally important: submarine fibre-optic cables carry 99% of global data traffic, with India connected through 14 landing stations, including those at Kochi and Thiruvananthapuram...
